title: Artificial airway suctioning

sources.use: AARC 2022 artificial airway suctioning CPG (cite only; permission needed to reproduce)
tracheostomy suctioning section (local NHS board guideline, past its review date)

objectives: Explain when to suction and why a fixed schedule is not the default.
Describe preoxygenation, event duration and saline use according to the guideline.
Monitor and escalate during and after suctioning.

items.text: Assess for retained secretions, changed breath sounds and secretion-associated ventilator waveform changes; suction for clinical indications rather than treating the clock as an indication. Adult-specific evidence on optimal suction frequency is limited.

Preoxygenation is recommended before artificial-airway suctioning in adults. Individualize the oxygen strategy to the patient's current oxygenation, support and the authorised local protocol; the guideline does not establish one fixed increase for every adult. Reassess oxygenation afterwards.
Do not routinely instil normal saline (evidence level B): it may worsen oxygenation and cause coughing, bronchospasm and rises in heart rate and ICP.
Use sterile technique for open suctioning (evidence level C); either open or closed systems can be used in adults; SHEA 2022 makes no VAP recommendation for closed systems.
Keep each event as brief as possible, no longer than 15 seconds (guideline text; the appropriateness score differs between sections).
Use the trained, device-appropriate shallow suction technique first; deeper suction is reserved for situations where shallower suction is ineffective. Do not force a catheter against resistance.
Explain to the patient, give analgesia or sedation per orders when needed, position appropriately, and perform hand hygiene on entering and leaving the area and immediately before open suctioning.

For a patient with a tracheostomy, suction only when needed after encouraging deep breaths and coughing, change a fenestrated inner cannula to a non-fenestrated one first, and treat difficulty passing the catheter as a possible blocked, misplaced or badly orientated tube, which is an emergency (NHS board guideline; see SK-05).
The nurse's role in suctioning varies by country and unit; follow local policy and competence requirements.
Suction system, catheter size and suction pressure follow the unit's policy; the catheter-size ratio is inconsistent within the guideline.
Check SpO2, heart rate, rhythm, ventilator pressures, secretions, and ICP and CPP where monitored.
Technique steps (depth, withdrawal, passes) follow the unit's approved procedure; the sections read do not specify them.
During and after suctioning: SpO2 and heart rate continuously, blood pressure as indicated, ECG rhythm, ventilator pressures and waveform, secretions, comfort and the number and duration of passes.
Stop and escalate for persistent desaturation, instability or arrhythmia, bleeding, suspected tube obstruction or displacement, bronchospasm, ICP rises or secretions that cannot be cleared.
Hypoxaemia, arrhythmias, bradycardia, hypotension or hypertension, raised ICP, bleeding and mucosal injury, bronchospasm, atelectasis, infection, pain, accidental extubation or disconnection.
Record the indication, pre-assessment, preoxygenation, system used, passes and duration, secretions, response and escalation per your unit's documentation standard.

checklist.text: Confirm a clinical indication, including secretion burden or related ventilator changes, and explain to the patient.
Perform hand hygiene and prepare equipment using sterile technique for open suctioning.
Use the individualized authorised preoxygenation strategy and reassess afterwards; do not apply a fixed oxygen increase to every patient.
Limit each suctioning event to as short a time as possible, no longer than 15 seconds.
Watch SpO2, heart rate, rhythm and pressures throughout, and afterwards.
Stop and call for help for persistent desaturation, instability, bleeding or suspected obstruction.
Record indication, passes, secretions and the patient's response.
Use trained shallow suction first; deeper suction only when the initial approach is ineffective. Never force a catheter against resistance; escalate suspected obstruction or displacement.

gaps: Adult as-needed frequency: no adult study found.
Catheter-size ratio and suction pressure: inconsistent or unspecified.
Suctioning in raised ICP: not covered. Tracheostomy suctioning rests on one local NHS board guideline (see SK-05).
